'''Timothy Scott Couch''' (born July 31, 1977) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[quarterback]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for five seasons with the [[Cleveland Browns]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Kentucky Wildcats football|Kentucky Wildcats]], winning [[Kellen Moore Award|Quarterback of the Year]] in 1998 after setting the [[Southeastern Conference]] record for single-season passing yards. Selected [[list of first overall National Football League draft picks|first overall]] by the Browns in the [[1999 NFL draft]], Couch was the franchise's first draft pick following their reactivation as an [[expansion team]].

Couch threw for over 11,000 passing yards and helped the Browns qualify for the postseason in 2002, but his career would be cut short by injuries. Following attempted comebacks with the [[Green Bay Packers]] and [[Jacksonville Jaguars]], he retired after failing to make the final roster for either team. Although Couch was unable to duplicate his college success, he was the first quarterback to lead the Browns to the playoffs since their NFL return and the only to do so between 2002 and 2019. He was inducted to the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2024.

'''Thurman Lee Thomas''' (born May 16, 1966) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[running back]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 13 seasons, primarily with the [[Buffalo Bills]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Oklahoma State Cowboys football|Oklahoma State Cowboys]], earning [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors twice. Thomas was selected by the Bills in the second round of the [[1988 NFL draft]], where he spent all but one season of his professional career. In his final season, he was a member of the [[Miami Dolphins]].

During his 12 seasons with the Bills, Thomas established himself as a central contributor of the Bills [[hurry-up offense#Development as a standard method|"K-Gun" offense]] that utilized no-huddle shotgun formations. He was named [[National Football League Most Valuable Player Award|NFL MVP]] in 1991, in addition to receiving five [[Pro Bowl]] and two first-team [[All-Pro]] selections. Thomas' efforts helped his team make a record four consecutive [[Super Bowl]] appearances from 1991 to 1994, although the Bills lost each game. He was inducted to the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2007 and the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2008.

'''Atiim Kiambu''' "'''Tiki'''" '''Barber Sr.'''<ref name="Football Reference">{{Cite web |title=Tiki Barber Stats - Pro-Football-Reference.com |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BarbTi00.htm |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |access-date=March 30, 2018 |archive-date=February 10, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180210032652/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BarbTi00.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|t|iː|k|i}}; born April 7, 1975) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who spent his entire 10-year career as a [[running back]] for the [[New York Giants]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Virginia Cavaliers football|Virginia Cavaliers]]. Barber was selected by the Giants in the second round of the [[1997 NFL draft]]. He retired from the NFL at the end of the 2006 NFL postseason as the Giants' all-time rushing and reception leader. He is the only player in NFL history to have 10,000 rushing yards, 5,000 receiving yards, and 1,000 return yards.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fennelly |first=John |date=December 1, 2023 |title=Giants great Tiki Barber just wants fair consideration for Hall of Fame |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/giants-great-tiki-barber-just-101553961.html |access-date=September 13, 2025 |website=Yahoo Sports |language=en-US |archive-date=September 28, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250928092126/https://sports.yahoo.com/giants-great-tiki-barber-just-101553961.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Barber was inducted into the [[Virginia Sports Hall of Fame and Museum|Virginia Sports Hall of Fame]] in 2011.

After his playing career, Barber became a national media presence, joining [[NBC]]'s ''[[The Today Show]]'' as a correspondent in 2007, then ''[[Football Night in America]]/[[NBC Sunday Night Football|Sunday Night Football]]''.<ref name="AP">Associated Press. [https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2763247 Barber to appear on 'Today,' NBC football] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250606185140/https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2763247 |date=June 6, 2025 }} ''ESPN.com'', February 12, 2007.</ref> He has published several children's books with [[identical twin]] brother [[Ronde Barber]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=January 31, 2017 |title=9 Football Books Kids Will Love by Tiki and Ronde Barber |url=https://www.helpingkidsrise.org/post/football-books-kids-will-love-by-tiki-and-ronde-barber |access-date=December 24, 2025 |website=Helping Kids Rise |language=en}}</ref> including ''By My Brother's Side'' (2004).<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Tiki & Ronde Barber to Publish Children’s Book |url=https://virginiasports.com/news/2003/04/09/tiki-amp-ronde-barber-to-publish-children-s-book |access-date=December 24, 2025 |website=Virginia Cavaliers Official Athletic Site |language=en-US}}</ref>

'''Timothy L. Bowens''' (born February 7, 1973) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive tackle]] for 11 seasons with the [[Miami Dolphins]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Ole Miss Rebels football|Ole Miss Rebels]], and was chosen with the 20th pick of the [[1994 NFL draft]] by the Dolphins.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1994 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1994/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

The Dolphins were initially criticized for picking Bowens, as he was overweight and had played only nine games in his college career at Mississippi.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20120526155219/http://articles.orlandosentinel.com/1994-12-28/sports/9412280072_1_tim-bowens-dolphins-defensive-tackle ''Orlando Sentinel'' 28 December 1994]</ref> He had a terrific rookie season in 1994, and Bowens was named 'The [[NFL Rookie of the Year Award|NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year]]' by the [[Associated Press]].<ref>[https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BoweTi00.htm Pro-Football Reference]</ref> He played with the Miami Dolphins for 11 years<ref>[http://www.nfl.com/player/timbowens/2499732/profile "Profile: Tim Bowens"], NFL</ref> before he retired after the [[2004 NFL season]]. He was inducted into the [[Miami Dolphins Honor Roll]] on October 27, 2024.

[[Memphis Catholic High School|Memphis Catholic]] {{nowrap|([[Memphis, Tennessee]])}} | college = [[Memphis Tigers football|Memphis]] | draftyear = 1986 | draftround = 4 | draftpick = 84 | pastteams = * [[Green Bay Packers]] ({{NFL Year|1986|1990}}) * [[San Francisco 49ers]] ({{NFL Year|1991|1992}}) * [[Philadelphia Eagles]] ({{NFL Year|1993}}) * San Francisco 49ers ({{NFL Year|1994|1995}}) | highlights = * [[Super Bowl champion]] ([[Super Bowl XXIX|XXIX]]) * First-team [[All-Pro]] ([[1989 All-Pro Team|1989]]) * Second-team All-Pro ([[1988 All-Pro Team|1988]]) * [[Pro Bowl]] ([[1990 Pro Bowl|1989]]) * First Team All-South Independent ([[1984 All-South Independent football team|1983, 1984]]) * [[Green Bay Packers Hall of Fame]] | statlabel1 = [[Tackle (football move)|Tackles]] | statvalue1 = 537 | statlabel2 = [[Quarterback sack|Sacks]] | statvalue2 = 81.0 | statlabel3 = [[Fumble]] recoveries | statvalue3 = 8 | pfr = HarrTi00 }} '''Timothy David Harris''' (born September 10, 1964) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] and [[defensive end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Green Bay Packers]] (1986–1990), the [[San Francisco 49ers]] (1991–1992, 1994–1995), and the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] (1993). He played [[college football]] at the [[University of Memphis]] and was selected by the Packers in the fourth round of the [[1986 NFL draft]].{{cite web |last=Hendricks |first=Martin |date=2014-06-19 |title=Former linebacker Tim Harris spent career getting into opponents' heads |url=https://archive.jsonline.com/sports/packers/former-linebacker-tim-harris-spent-career-getting-into-opponents-heads-b99290909z1-263862331.html |access-date=2025-10-02 |website=Milwaukee Journal Sentinel}}{{Cite web |title=1986 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1986/draft.htm |access-date=2023-10-02 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} As he entered Birmingham's Woodlawn High School, he began to excel in both football and basketball, but he moved with his aunt and uncle, who were teachers, to Memphis after his junior season. "My grades were not so good (at Woodlawn High) and I was not hanging around with the right people," Harris said. "And my mom and I thought I'd get more exposure in Memphis." [1] Harris attended Memphis Catholic High School, but he was ineligible for most of the football season because of the move. Catholic High made the playoffs and Harris was finally declared eligible. In his one and only game for Catholic, Harris recorded 22 tackles and caught the attention of major college coaches, including those at UCLA, Notre Dame and Tennessee. But he chose to stay close to home and play for the [[Memphis Tigers Football|University of Memphis Tigers]], where he was part of the nation's top-ranked defense for two seasons in 1984 and 85. In The NFL, Harris was a key defensive player for a Packers team that finished 10-6 during the [[1989 Green Bay Packers season|1989 season]], their best record since 1972. The team was referred to as the "Cardiac Pack" because of several close game wins. Harris finished that season with a career best 19.5 [[Quarterback sack|sacks]] and was selected to the [[Pro Bowl]]. Later in his career, he recorded 17 sacks as part of the [[1992 San Francisco 49ers season|1992 San Francisco team]] that reached the [[NFC Championship Game]]. Two seasons later, he would earn a [[Super Bowl ring]] as the 49ers won [[Super Bowl XXIX]]. Harris was a talkative, outgoing player, whose signature celebration after a sack was "six gun" hand gestures, whereby he pretended to shoot the opposing player. The NFL eventually banned his celebration as overly aggressive and unsportsmanlike. During a Chicago Bears game in 1987 at Soldier Field, Harris and a young pair of Bears fans almost got into a fight over a flattened cup that was thrown directly at Harris. After the NFL and Pete Rozelle investigated the incident, it was determined that no disciplinary action would take place against Harris for the outburst. In 2022, Harris was inducted into the [[Green Bay Packers Hall of Fame]].{{cite web | last=Ryman | first=Richard | title=Tim Harris, Greg Jennings join Green Bay Packers Hall of Fame | website=USA TODAY | date=2022-09-02 | url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/2022/09/01/tim-harris-greg-jennings-join-green-bay-packers-hall-fame/7893993001/ | access-date=2025-08-29}}

'''William Tim Anderson''' (born August 1, 1949) is an American former professional [[Gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[defensive back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) and [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL). He played for the [[Toronto Argonauts]], [[San Francisco 49ers]] and [[Buffalo Bills]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State Buckeyes]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://buckeyextra.dispatch.com/content/stories/2012/11/09/gameday/history.html|title = History.HTML}}</ref>

After being drafted by the 49ers in the first round of the [[1971 NFL draft]], Anderson was so unhappy with the 49ers' contract offer that he considered quitting football and signed with the Argonauts instead.<ref name=dream>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2022-09-03|newspaper=Ithaca Journal|title=He kept his dream: Canada to the 49ers|date=September 1, 1975|page=13|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/108884068/the-ithaca-journal/}}</ref>  Anderson said that "The negotiations with the 49ers go off on the wrong foot and got progressively worse."<ref name=dream/>  He believed that he was the first NFL first round draft pick to sign with the CFL instead (but he was not as that was [[Johnny Bright]] who was selected 5th in 1952, and many other players followed), and was followed by [[Heisman Trophy]] winner [[Johnny Rodgers]] in 1973 in taking that route.<ref name=dream/> He earned all-CFL honors while with the Argonauts in 1973.<ref name=dream/><ref>{{cite web|title=William Anderson|url=https://www.statscrew.com/football/stats/p-anderwil002|publisher=Stats Crew|accessdate=2022-09-03}}</ref>  He signed with the 49ers before the 1975 season and said that the contract was "for a lot better money than they offered [in 1971], but it's not a no-cut contract."<ref name=dream/>

After serving as a backup [[Safety (gridiron football position)|safety]] for most of the 1975 season, Anderson and [[Mike Holmes (wide receiver)|Mike Holmes]] were traded to the Bills in exchange for 2 draft picks before the 1976 season.<ref>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2022-09-03|newspaper=Concord Transcript|date=September 7, 1976|title=Niners deal with Bills|page=6|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/108884864/concord-transcript/}}</ref> After playing the first two games for the Bills in September 1976, he was placed on [[injured reserve]] with a bruised thigh and the Bills then waived him in October.<ref>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2022-09-03|newspaper=Valley Morning Star|date=September 25, 1976|title=Bills waive Vic Washington|page=B4|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/108885121/valley-morning-star/}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2022-09-03|newspaper=Democrat and Chronicle|date=October 8, 1976|title=Bills start Edwards|author=Pascarelli, Peter|page=3D|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/108885467/democrat-and-chronicle/}}</ref> The [[Detroit Lions]] signed Anderson before the 1977 season but waived him during preseason.<ref>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2022-09-03|newspaper=Johnson City Press|date=June 24, 1977|title=Lions sign Tim Anderson|page=17|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/108885692/johnson-city-press/}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|accessdate=2022-09-03|newspaper=Herald-Palladium|date=September 2, 1977|title=Lions get Mike-Mayer|page=17|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/108885909/the-herald-palladium/}}</ref>

'''Timothy John Foley''' (born May 30, 1958) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive tackle]] for the [[Baltimore Colts]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame Fighting Irish]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Tim Foley Stats, News and Video –  T|url=https://www.nfl.com/players/tim-foley/|access-date=2021-05-26|website=NFL.com}}</ref>

Foley was a three-year starter at the [[University of Notre Dame]] under head coach [[Dan Devine]]. Foley played left tackle and blocked for quarterback [[Joe Montana]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Jablonski|first=David|title=Rise of the Irish brings back memories for Foley|url=https://www.springfieldnewssun.com/sports/college/rise-the-irish-brings-back-memories-for-foley/rUlX0675MzKh9auorhKg7M/|access-date=2021-05-26|website=springfield-news-sun}}</ref> In 1977, the Fighting Irish were voted consensus [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|national champions]] after defeating the previously unbeaten and No. 1 ranked [[Texas Longhorns football|Texas Longhorns]] in the [[1977 Cotton Bowl Classic|Cotton Bowl Classic]]. During his senior year, Foley was named a team captain, along with running back [[Vagas Ferguson]] and safety [[Dave Waymer]]. Foley was a consensus [[College Football All-America Team|College Football All-America team]] selection in 1979.

Foley was selected in the second round of the [[1980 NFL draft]] by the [[Baltimore Colts]]. After three seasons with the Colts, he ended his professional football career in 1982.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Timothy Foley|url=http://www.foleybenefitsgroup.com/team/timothy-foley|access-date=2021-05-26|website=foleybenefitsgroup.com}}</ref>

Currently, Foley works at a life insurance and health group benefits company with his brother [[Dave Foley (American football)|Dave Foley]], who is a [[1968 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|1968 National Champion]] for the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State Buckeyes]] and a former professional [[offensive lineman]]. Foley Benefits Group, LLC is based in [[Springfield, Ohio]].
